chunks: And ʿUmar ibn Udhaynah narrated from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said:
I asked him about garlic, so he said:

The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله only forbade it because of its smell, and he said: Whoever eats this foul plant should not come near our mosque. But as for one who eats it and does not come to the mosque, there is no harm.

key_terms.الْبَقْلَةَ الْخَبِيثَةَ: the foul plant, referring here to garlic because of its odor
key_terms.رَسُولُ اللَّهِ: the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله

ai.seo_question: Is eating garlic forbidden in Islam, or is the ruling only about coming to the mosque with its smell?
ai.summary: This hadith explains that the prohibition regarding garlic is not absolute, but is connected to its offensive smell in the mosque. It establishes an etiquette-based legal ruling: eating it is not itself forbidden, but attending the mosque after eating it is blameworthy due to causing discomfort to others.

en.bab-ul-qaim-publications: Hadith.4269 - Umar ibn Udhaynah narrated from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far Imam Muhammad ibn Ali Al-Baqir (as), who said:

I asked him about garlic.
Imam (as) said:

"The Messenger of Allah (swt) (peace be upon him and his family) only forbade it because of its smell.
Prophet (sw) said: 'Whoever eats this foul plant should not come near our mosque.' However, as for one who eats it and does not go to the mosque, there is no harm."
